## Climatological Context and Study Area Description

Bandar Abbas, the capital of Hormozgan Province in southern Iran on the coast of the Persian Gulf, features a hot desert/semi-arid climate characterized by extremely high summer temperatures and intense relative humidity.

In this study, I analyzed the trends of key temperature parameters and the Heat Index for Bandar Abbas over a 13-year period (2013–2025) using daily meteorological records. The objective of this report is to deliver a structured, data-driven statistical analysis suitable for evaluating localized climate dynamics and environmental risks.

## Long-Term Temperature Trend Analysis (2013–2025)

To extract long-term temperature signals from seasonal noise, I applied non-parametric LOESS (Locally Estimated Scatterplot Smoothing) to the daily mean temperature time series. The smoothed curve reveals long-term thermal variability across the study period, with the smoothed baseline temperature increasing from approximately 26.0 °C in 2013, stabilizing around 27.5 °C to 28.5 °C between 2015 and 2024, and rising sharply toward over 31.0 °C by late 2025, while daily mean temperatures span from approximately 14.0 °C to 18.0 °C during winter troughs to approximately 36.0 °C to 38.5 °C at summer peaks.

![](../result/bandar-abbas/long-term%20temperature%20overview%20(2013–2025).png)

## Seasonal Dynamics and Ramadan Temperature Anomalies

The 2024 daily mean temperature time series clearly demonstrates the expected sinusoidal seasonal cycle. To evaluate temperature anomalies during specific temporal windows, I calculated the 30-day rolling average temperature on the final day of Ramadan and compared it against historical data for the same calendar date across all study years. For 2025, with Ramadan spanning from February 28 to March 29, the 30-day rolling average on the final day (March 29, 2025) was recorded at 24.43 °C, which is higher than the historical mean of 23.31 °C for that calendar date.

![](../result/bandar-abbas/yearly%20temperature%20(2024).png)

![](../result/bandar-abbas/30-day%20Rolling%20Avg%20on%20Last%20Day%20of%20Ramadan%202025%20vs%20Past%20Years.png)

## Monthly Heat Index Trends and Statistical Testing

By fitting Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression models and executing the non-parametric Mann-Kendall (MK) test on monthly mean Heat Index values, I evaluated long-term thermal trends for each month across the 13-year study period (2013–2025). Statistically significant upward trends were identified in four of the twelve months:

**June**: Regression slope of +0.29 °C/year (cumulative change ≈ +3.48 °C, $\text{lm\_p} = 0.0059$, $\text{mk\_p} = 0.0060$, $\tau = 0.590$).

**July**: Regression slope of +0.29 °C/year (cumulative change ≈ +3.42 °C, $\text{lm\_p} = 0.0029$, $\text{mk\_p} = 0.0060$, $\tau = 0.590$).

**August**: Regression slope of +0.28 °C/year (cumulative change ≈ +3.30 °C, $\text{lm\_p} = 0.0053$, $\text{mk\_p} = 0.0327$, $\tau = 0.462$).

**November**: Regression slope of +0.27 °C/year (cumulative change ≈ +3.22 °C, $\text{lm\_p} = 0.0038$, $\text{mk\_p} = 0.0041$, $\tau = 0.615$).

September exhibited a weak or oscillating trend (slope of +0.24 °C/year, cumulative change ≈ +2.85 °C, $\text{lm\_p} = 0.0418$, but non-significant $\text{mk\_p} = 0.0995$). In the remaining seven months, no statistically significant trends were detected ($p > 0.05$).

The pronounced summer Heat Index increases (June through August) severely aggravate urban bioclimatic stress, outdoor worker safety hazards, and peak cooling power grid demand in coastal Bandar Abbas, while marked late-autumn warming in November delays seasonal cooling and extends humid summer-like conditions into late autumn.

**Statistical Terminology & Methodological Note:**

**$p$-value ($\text{lm\_p}$ / $\text{mk\_p}$)**: A measure of statistical significance representing the probability that an observed trend occurred due to random variability. A threshold of $p < 0.05$ denotes a statistically significant trend at the 95% confidence level.

**Mann-Kendall Test (MK / $\text{mk\_p}$)**: A non-parametric rank correlation test used in climatology to confirm whether a monotonic upward or downward trend exists without assuming a normal data distribution.

**Kendall’s Tau ($\tau$ / $\text{mk\_tau}$)**: A non-parametric correlation coefficient ranging from $-1$ to $+1$ that measures the strength and direction of a monotonic trend (positive values indicate an upward trajectory).

**Classification Criteria**: A monthly warming trend is classified as statistically significant only when both the OLS regression ($\text{lm\_p} < 0.05$) and the Mann-Kendall test ($\text{mk\_p} < 0.05$) indicate significant upward shifts.

**Note on Monthly Heat Index Plots**: Blue points represent years with a mean Heat Index at or below the overall multi-year average, while red points represent years above the overall average.

## Extreme Temperature Event Assessment

I defined extreme temperature days as those exceeding two standard deviations (±2 SD) from the 30-day rolling mean
. Based on this threshold, November recorded the highest overall frequency of extreme days in Bandar Abbas, totaling 78 days (all 78 being very cold anomalies relative to the rolling baseline). October followed with 56 days (all very cold), April with 48 days (all very hot), December with 44 days (all very cold), and January with 42 days (all very cold).

Very hot extreme days were concentrated in spring and early summer, occurring most frequently in April (48 days)
, followed by March, May, and June (39 days each).

February recorded 27 extreme-temperature days (8 very cold and 19 very hot days), indicating substantial variability in the occurrence of temperature extremes. The presence of both categories within the same month highlights the need to examine the timing, intensity, and potential implications of these extremes in Bandar Abbas.


![](../result/bandar-abbas/extreme%20temperature%20days%20by%20month%20(hot%20vs%20cold).png)

## Annual Share of Ramadan Extremes vs. Full Year

I evaluated the proportion of annual extreme temperature days occurring specifically within Ramadan relative to full-year totals in Bandar Abbas. Across the 13-year study period (2013–2025), extreme temperature days occurred during Ramadan in nearly every year, peaking in 2017 with 8 extreme days out of 39 total annual extremes. For instance, in 2018, 5 of the 44 total annual extreme temperature days coincided with the month of Ramadan.

![](../result/bandar-abbas/year-by-year%20comparison%20-%20Extreme%20days%20in%20Ramadan%20vs.%20full%20year.png)
